rows.verified: Respiratory protective equipment should be used only after other reasonably practicable exposure controls have been applied.
RPE must be adequate, providing the protection needed to reduce exposure in line with legal requirements.
RPE must be suitable for the wearer, the task and the working environment.
RPE selection, use and maintenance must be handled by properly trained people.
RPE must be maintained, examined, tested and stored correctly, with required records retained.
Each wearer must be fit-tested for each tight-fitting facepiece they use.
Selected RPE must work correctly with other protective equipment worn at the same time.
An effective RPE programme includes selection, training, supervision, pre-use checks, maintenance, record keeping, storage and disposal.
RPE performance depends on contaminant, concentration, protection factor, face fit, wearer condition, task, maintenance and correct use.
HSE RPE evidence is substance-, device-, wearer-, task-, fit-, maintenance- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory-disease probability.
Employers must control health risks from welding fume for specialist and occasional welding work.
HSE states that all welding fume can cause lung cancer.
Welding fume can also cause occupational asthma and other health conditions.
A welding-fume risk assessment should consider the process, work volume, fume level, component size, metal and consumable.
Controls should first consider avoiding or reducing exposure through alternative joining or lower-fume processes.
Local exhaust ventilation should capture welding fume at source where possible.
Suitable respiratory protective equipment is required where exposure is not adequately controlled by other measures.
Control measures and general ventilation must be maintained, and welders must understand risks and correct control use.
Welding-fume risk depends on process, metal, consumable, coating, duration, ventilation, extraction, RPE and worker susceptibility.
HSE welding evidence is process-, material-, welder-, ventilation-, control-, exposure- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level cancer probability.
Ionising radiation includes X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive sources and naturally occurring sources such as radon.
Employers must manage ionising-radiation risks to protect workers and members of the public.
Low-risk work requires notification, medium-risk work requires registration and high-risk work requires consent.
The principal HSE-enforced legal requirements are the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017.
Radiation exposure must be kept as low as reasonably practicable and must not exceed specified dose limits.
